A decoder-only language model is a probability distribution implemented as a stack of repeated tensor operations. Understanding those operations is necessary for interpreting every later decision about data, systems, scaling, and post-training.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. convert documents into packed input and target token sequences;
2. derive the shapes and computation of causal multi-head self-attention;
3. explain residual streams, normalization, RoPE, and gated feed-forward layers;
4. calculate parameters, activation memory, attention memory, and approximate FLOPs; and
5. implement and test a minimal GPT block in PyTorch.

## The tokenizer–model boundary

Raw text first becomes token IDs. Subword tokenization trades vocabulary size against sequence length: frequent strings receive compact representations while rare strings are composed from smaller units. [SentencePiece](https://aclanthology.org/D18-2012/) [@kudo2018sentencepiece] is one reproducible way to train such a vocabulary directly from raw sentences.

For a packed sequence

```text
<BOS> data quality matters <EOS>
```

causal language modeling shifts the target by one position:

```text
Input:   <BOS> data    quality matters
Target:  data  quality matters <EOS>
```

Document separators, padding, conversation-control tokens, and loss masks are therefore architectural inputs as well as data choices.

## Embeddings and the residual stream

Each token ID selects a vector from an embedding matrix. The resulting sequence has shape $X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d}$ for batch size $B$, sequence length $T$, and model width $d$. Transformer sublayers do not replace this representation. They write updates into a **residual stream**:

$$
X' = X + \operatorname{Attention}(\operatorname{Norm}(X)),
$$

$$
X'' = X' + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{Norm}(X')).
$$

This pre-normalization form is common in modern decoder-only models. Exact normalization, activation, bias, and initialization choices belong to the model specification and affect training stability.

## Causal self-attention

For one attention head, learned projections produce queries, keys, and values:

$$
Q=XW_Q,\qquad K=XW_K,\qquad V=XW_V.
$$

Scaled dot-product attention is

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}}+M\right)V,
$$

where $d_h$ is the head dimension and $M$ contains $-\infty$ above the causal diagonal. The mask ensures that position $t$ cannot use target tokens at positions greater than $t$.

Multi-head attention reshapes projections to $B\times H\times T\times d_h$, applies attention per head, concatenates the results, and uses an output projection to return to width $d$. [*Attention Is All You Need*](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/7181-attention-is-all-you-need.pdf) [@vaswani2017attention] introduced the general mechanism; decoder-only GPT systems retain the causal self-attention portion.

## Position and feed-forward computation

Attention alone is permutation-equivariant, so the model needs position information. Rotary position embeddings, or [RoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864) [@su2021rope], rotate query and key coordinates according to token position, making relative offsets accessible to their dot products.

The feed-forward sublayer applies the same nonlinear transformation at every position. A gated variant such as SwiGLU computes a product between an activated branch and a linear branch before projecting back to the residual width. [LLaMA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971) [@touvron2023llama] provides a useful open specification combining pre-normalization, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and RoPE.

## The language-model objective

For tokens $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the model factorizes

$$
p(x_1,\ldots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
$$

Training minimizes mean negative log-likelihood over unmasked target positions:

$$
\mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
$$

At inference time, the same model samples or selects one token, appends it to the context, and repeats. Training processes many target positions in parallel; autoregressive generation is sequential across newly produced tokens.

## Resource accounting

Before running the model, estimate:

- parameters in embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and output head;
- parameter, gradient, and optimizer-state memory;
- activation memory as a function of $B$, $T$, layers, and width;
- the $T^2$ attention-score term; and
- approximate training FLOPs per token and per step.

An estimate should be close enough to explain an out-of-memory error or an implausible throughput claim. Lecture 8 will replace several naive operations with memory-efficient kernels and distributed execution.

## Studio: implement the block

Implement token embedding, RMSNorm, causal multi-head attention, a SwiGLU feed-forward layer, one Transformer block, and an output projection. The submission includes unit tests for tensor shapes, future-token masking, parameter sharing, deterministic generation, and checkpoint save/load.

Finally, overfit one short batch. Failure to drive the loss near zero is a diagnostic: the bug may be in target shifting, the causal mask, normalization, the optimizer, or generation—not in insufficient data.

## What to remember

1. Tokenization and packing determine the sequences the architecture receives.
2. Causal attention mixes information only from the current and previous positions.
3. Residual blocks repeatedly add attention and feed-forward updates to one stream.
4. RoPE, normalization, and gated MLPs are explicit, testable model choices.
5. Parameter, memory, and FLOP estimates should be written before the training run.
6. A tiny-data overfit test is the first end-to-end correctness check.
